name: Tranexamic acid oral

card.summary: An antifibrinolytic tablet used off-label by dermatologists to lighten melasma, the dark facial patches that make skin tone look uneven.
card.note: Prescription-only in most countries; contraindicated with a history of blood clots or seizures.

quick.overview:
Oral tranexamic acid (TXA) is a synthetic lysine analogue first made in 1962 by Shosuke and Utako Okamoto and long used to reduce bleeding [1]. Dermatologists in many countries also prescribe it off-label for melasma, a chronic hyperpigmentation condition that commonly affects the cheeks and forehead.

The appearance payoff is more even skin tone. A 2018 review reported clear efficacy in Asian skin at low doses over 8 to 12 weeks [2], and a 2018 randomized placebo-controlled study examined moderate-to-severe melasma [9]. Expert consensus recognizes it as one option within a wider melasma plan that also relies on sun protection [5].
quick.how: It is taken by mouth under a doctor's supervision, usually alongside sun protection and topical lightening agents, and sometimes with lasers or peels. Dermatology reviews describe a screening of clotting history before prescribing.
quick.risks: Reported effects include stomach upset, menstrual changes and rare allergic reactions; blood clots, seizures and visual changes are rare. Reviews of melasma use report that it did not increase thromboembolic risk, but patients are screened for risk factors [2]. It is contraindicated with a history of clots or seizures and is prescription-only in the US [1].

lead: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that stops plasmin forming and thereby slows the breakdown of blood clots; it is on the WHO list of essential medicines and is used for trauma, surgery, dental work and heavy menstrual bleeding [1]. Its use in skin lightening for melasma is off-label, and Japan allows it as a quasi-drug for skin whitening [1].

Melasma is a chronic acquired hyperpigmentation disorder with high relapse rates, and dermatologists treat it with sun protection and combinations of topicals, peels and lasers [3][4]. Oral TXA is described as a multimodal option that acts on the skin's pigment pathways [2].

A network meta-analysis of six randomized trials with 599 patients sought the best oral dose [6], and randomized trials have compared oral with topical TXA [7] and combined oral TXA with triple cream [8].

chain: Interferes with pigment-stimulating pathways in skin
angle.text: Patients with stubborn melasma take it on prescription to lighten dark patches on the face. It is usually added to sun protection and topical treatment.

infobox: Rx in US; pharmacy medicine for heavy periods in UK [1]

paras: For melasma, oral TXA is prescribed for cases not responding to topical therapy [2]. A 2024 review lists it among recent developments alongside visible-light photoprotection, non-hydroquinone agents, peels and lasers [3].
It is approved for heavy menstrual bleeding in the US (Lysteda, 2009), and used in trauma, postpartum hemorrhage and surgery [1][4].

A review concluded that low-dose oral TXA over 8 to 12 weeks is efficacious in refractory melasma in Asian skin [2]. A 2022 trial tested oral TXA added to a fluocinolone-based triple cream against the cream alone [8]. A 2021 phase II trial examined its effect on erythema index in melasma patients [10]. An international Delphi consensus of 38 dermatologists in 2026 addressed melasma management broadly [5].

Reported effects are generally mild; rare events include seizures, visual changes and clotting [1]. Whether it raises clot risk is debated and large studies have not shown increases [1]. Contraindications include prior thromboembolism, seizure history and severe kidney impairment [1].
TXA binds lysine sites on plasminogen, reducing plasmin formation [1]. The skin effect is described as multimodal, involving the plasminogen-melanocyte pathway [2].

Randomized trials in melasma include a placebo-controlled study of oral TXA for moderate-to-severe disease [9], a comparison of oral and topical TXA [7], and a trial adding oral TXA to triple cream [8]. A network meta-analysis of six randomized trials examined dose [6]. Results vary, and reviews note relapse after stopping is common in melasma generally [3].

timeline.event: Synthesized by Shosuke and Utako Okamoto [1].
FDA approves oral Lysteda for heavy menstrual bleeding [1].
Review and randomized placebo-controlled study of oral TXA for melasma published [2][9].
